questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at $a$ with $\nabla f(a)\ne0$. Which formula always gives the unit vector maximising $D_uf(a)$, regardless of the nonzero gradient?
options: $e_i$, where $i$ indexes a largest partial derivative

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at $a$, with nonzero gradient and maximal unit-direction rate $M=\|\nabla f(a)\|$. A unit vector $u$ makes an angle of $\pi/3$ with the gradient. What is $D_uf(a)$?
A differentiable function $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ has $\nabla f(a)=(-3,4)$. Which unit direction gives the fastest decrease at $a$?
Suppose $f\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, with $n\ge2$, is differentiable at $a$ and $\nabla f(a)=0$. What does first-order information say about a steepest ascent direction at $a$?
options: The point $a$ must be a local maximum of $f$.
The steepest ascent direction is the zero vector.
Only coordinate directions maximise the directional derivative.
All directional derivatives are 0; no direction stands out.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at $a$, and write $g=\nabla f(a)\ne0$. Which argument establishes $D_uf(a)\le\|g\|$ for every unit vector $u$?
options: Equality $g\cdot u=\|g\|\|u\|$ holds for all unit vectors $u$.

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=x^2y$, which unit vector is the steepest ascent direction at $(1,3)$?
For the linear function $f(x,y)=3x-4y$, what is the largest directional derivative at any point?
At $(1,2)$, what is the directional derivative of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ in the direction $u=-(1,2)/\sqrt5$?
In which unit direction does $f(x,y)=\mathrm{e}^{x}\sin y$ increase fastest at $(0,\pi/2)$?
On a plate with temperature $T(x,y)=100-x^2-2y^2$, an ant at $(1,1)$ wants to warm up as fast as possible. Which unit direction should it take?
Let $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable near $a$, with $\nabla f(a)\ne0$. How is the steepest ascent direction at $a$ related to the level curve $f(x,y)=f(a)$ through $a$?
options: It is tangent to the level curve.
It points towards the global maximum of $f$.
It always lies along the axis of the largest partial derivative.
It is perpendicular to the level curve.

questions.question: A hiker follows the current steepest ascent direction of a continuously differentiable height function $f(x,y)$, staying where $\nabla f\ne0$. Does the path have to be a straight line?
options: Yes, since the direction is fixed at the starting point.
Yes, along the straight line to the summit.
Not in general; $\nabla f/\|\nabla f\|$ can change along the path.
Only when $f$ is a quadratic function.

questions.question: Let $g=3f$ with $f$ differentiable and $\nabla f(a)\ne0$. How do the steepest ascent direction and maximal rate of $g$ at $a$ compare with those of $f$?
options: Same direction; the maximal rate is three times larger.
Same direction and the same maximal rate.
The direction is multiplied by 3; the rate is unchanged.
Opposite direction; the rate is three times larger.

questions.question: At a point $a$ in $\mathbb R^3$, $\nabla f(a)=(2,-1,2)$. What are the steepest ascent direction and the maximal rate of increase there?
For $f(x,y)=x^2+xy$ at $(1,1)$, in which unit directions is the directional derivative zero?
options: No unit direction gives rate zero.

questions.question: A hill has height $h(x,y)=1000-0.001x^2-0.002y^2$ (metres, with $x,y$ in metres). To two decimals, what is the steepest slope, in metres of height per metre, at $(100,50)$?

A differentiable function $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ is constant on the ellipse $x^2/4+y^2=2$. At $a=(2,1)$, its partial derivative is $f_x(a)=3$. What is its maximal directional derivative over unit vectors at $a$?
